PAPER: RESEARCH ARTICLE Published Online: November 25, 2025 https://doi.org/10.31893/multiscience.2026375 Time-varying value relevance of advertising expenditures around the COVID-19 pandemic: Evidence from the korean stock market Gee-Jung Kwona aHanbat National University, Republic of Korea. Abstract This study investigates the relationship between advertising expenditure and firm value in the context of Korean listed companies from 2018 to 2023, focusing on how this relationship evolves across different phases of the COVID-19 pandemic. The analysis divides the sample period into pre-COVID-19 (2018–2019), during COVID-19 (2020–2021), and post- COVID-19 (2022–2023). Advertising intensity is measured as the ratio of advertising expenses to total sales, and firm value is proxied by Tobin’s Q. Using multiple regression models with interaction terms and firm-level control variables such as leverage, profitability, growth potential, and governance, the study finds that advertising expenditure has a significantly positive effect on firm value across the full period. Notably, the positive effect becomes stronger during the pandemic, suggesting that advertising plays a vital role in enhancing or maintaining firm value under economic uncertainty. However, this effect diminishes in the post-COVID-19 period. These findings underscore the importance of adaptive advertising strategies that respond to changing external environments. The study contributes to the literature by highlighting the time- varying value relevance of advertising and offers practical insights for corporate managers and policymakers in periods of economic disruption. Keywords: advertising, Covid 19, value relevance, korean stock markets, advertising expenditure, firm value 1. Introduction In today’s highly competitive business environment, companies utilize a wide array of strategic resources to ensure survival and promote growth. Among these, advertising expenditure serves as a critical marketing tool that enhances consumer engagement, increases brand awareness (Keller, 1993; Keller and Lehmann, 2003; Kotler and Keller, 2012), and secures market share. Traditionally, advertising is understood as a strategy focused on boosting sales and influencing consumer behavior. However, empirical interest in how advertising expenditures affect firm value continues to grow (Barth et al., 2001; Joshi and Hanssens, 2010). Recent international studies have extended this discussion beyond the local context, examining various markets and crisis situations. For example, Joshi and Hanssens (2010) and Du (2020) find that advertising spending delivers a significant and enduring positive effect on firm valuation not only in the US but across multiple countries and industries. Li et al. (2022) demonstrate through a cross-national sample that the relationship between advertising expenditures and firm performance varies by a firm’s lifecycle and economic environment, while Han and Manry (2004) find robust effects in East Asian capital markets. In emerging markets, similar positive results reaffirm advertising’s universal value-enhancing role (Mirza and Gull, 2022). More broadly, international evidence highlights that advertising effectiveness depends on institutional, cultural, and macroeconomic settings, with studies reporting varying results across Europe (Dekimpe and Hanssens, 1999; Tellis and Tellis, 2009) and Latin America (Andras and Srinivasan, 2003). Such findings suggest that country-specific conditions moderate the extent to which advertising enhances firm value, emphasizing the importance of comparative perspectives. Especially in an environment where information asymmetry continues to decline and external communication strategies gain importance, advertising functions not only as a marketing tool but also as a signal to external stakeholders about a firm’s future earnings potential (Graham and Frankenberger, 2000). Accordingly, advertising expenditures convey positive signals to capital market participants, which reflect in stock prices and ultimately contribute to enhancing firm value (Aaker and Jacobson, 1994). However, advertising expenditure does not necessarily lead to an increase in firm value. Since advertising is inherently considered a cost, concerns about its effectiveness and efficiency persist. When its contribution to sales or profits is not clearly observable, excessive advertising spending may be perceived negatively by shareholders or investors (Lev and Thiagarajan, 1993), potentially resulting in a decline in firm value. For example, the COVID-19 pandemic, which begins in 2020, brings unprecedented disruptions to the global economy and industries at large (Donthu and Gustafsson, 2020), significantly changing consumer behavior, corporate strategy, and investment patterns. Consequently, firms readjust their advertising strategies, and the effect of advertising expenditure on firm value likely differs across periods (Kim et al., 2019). Similar to the 2008 global financial crisis, when firms’ advertising strategies shifted markedly due to liquidity constraints and demand shocks (Lamey et al., 2007), the COVID-19 period provides a natural experiment to examine the resilience and effectiveness of advertising in times of external shock. Based on these considerations, this study empirically analyzes the impact of advertising expenditure on firm value and examines how this relationship changes over time in the context of the external shock caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. The analysis covers the period from 2018 to 2023, which is segmented into three sub-periods: the pre-pandemic period (2018– 2019), the pandemic period (2020–2021), and the post-pandemic period (2022–2023). This study compares and analyzes the relationship between advertising expenditure and firm value across these periods to offer a comprehensive understanding of its temporal dynamics. This study provides both academic and practical contributions in several respects. First, while many prior studies focus on the impact of advertising expenditures on firms’ financial performance, this study differentiates itself by using Tobin’s Q— a market-based performance metric—to analyze the strategic impact of advertising (Chauvin and Hirschey, 1993). Second, rather than examining the relationship at a single point in time, this study investigates how it evolves across structurally distinct periods defined by the COVID-19 pandemic, thereby offering insights into the effectiveness of advertising strategies under different environmental conditions. Third, by conducting an empirical analysis of non-financial firms listed on the Korean stock market, this study provides practical implications for strategic advertising decisions in the domestic corporate context. In addition, by incorporating a wide range of firm-level controls—including leverage, ownership concentration, and market-to- book ratio as well as the ratios of intangible and tangible assets—this study accounts for structural characteristics that can influence firm valuation. The inclusion of these asset-related variables is consistent with international research emphasizing the role of resource allocation in shaping firm value (Hall, 1993 ; Corrado et al., 2005). As such, this study systematically investigates the impact of corporate advertising strategies on firm value under conditions of uncertainty and external volatility, offering valuable insights for both financial evaluation and strategic decision- making regarding advertising expenditures. The findings are expected to contribute not only to academic discussions on value relevance but also to managerial practices, particularly regarding budget allocation under crisis conditions. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews the literature on the relationship between advertising expenditure and firm value to establish the theoretical background. Section 3 presents the hypotheses and research models used to test them. Section 4 provides the empirical analysis and interprets the results. Finally, Section 5 concludes the study and discusses its implications and future research directions. 2. Theoretical Background Advertising serves as a core marketing activity through which firms inform consumers about their products or brands (Kotler and Keller, 2012) and enhance their competitiveness in the market. By investing in advertising, firms aim to influence consumer purchase intentions, increase brand loyalty, and ultimately improve financial performance such as expanded market share. Numerous theoretical and empirical studies support the notion that such advertising activities, similar to R&D expenditures, function as intangible assets that positively affect firm value over the long term (Barth et al., 2001; Chan et al., 2001). From a theoretical standpoint, this view is consistent with the resource-based view which regards firm-specific intangible resources (e.g., brand equity built by advertising) as drivers of sustained competitive advantage (Barney, 1991). In addition, the intangible-capital literature emphasizes that investments in non-physical assets (including advertising and marketing capabilities) may be value-relevant even when not fully recognized on financial statements (Corrado et al., 2005). The relationship between advertising expenditure and firm value remains a central topic in business, accounting, and marketing research. Early studies emphasize that advertising provides consumers with product information, enhances brand recognition, and ultimately contributes to increased revenue and profitability (Nelson, 1974; Milgrom and Roberts, 1986). In this context, Aaker and Jacobson (1994) empirically show that advertising influences perceived quality among consumers, which in turn reflects in market value indicators such as stock prices. Signaling theory also helps explain these mechanisms: when firms sustain or increase advertising, they may signal managerial confidence and future prospects to outside investors, thereby reducing information asymmetry and affecting market valuation (Spence, 1973; Graham & Frankenberger, 2000). Chauvin and Hirschey (1993) argue that both advertising and R&D expenditures positively influence firm market value. Similarly, Haryanto and Retnaningrum (2007) find that advertising spending significantly affects a firm’s profitability and growth potential. Joshi and Hanssens (2010) demonstrate that advertising not only increases sales but also has a long-term impact on firm value. These findings collectively suggest that advertising expenditures should be regarded not merely as costs, but as strategic investments. International research has also reinforced these findings by highlighting both direct and indirect channels through which advertising contributes to firm value. Graham and Frankenberger (2000) emphasize that increases in advertising expenditure https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj Kwon (2026) 3 influence not only short-term performance but also long-term stock prices, highlighting its importance in both accounting and market information. McAlister et al. (2007) further report that advertising can reduce systematic risk, thereby contributing positively to firm value. Joshi and Hanssens (2010) confirm that advertising impacts firm value both directly, through improved sales, and indirectly, through enhanced brand equity. More recently, Du (2020) provides evidence that advertising expenditures exert a direct positive effect on firm value, while Li et al. (2021) demonstrate that the valuation effects of advertising are particularly strong in emerging markets, underscoring the global relevance of this topic. At the same time, long-run marketing studies show that sustained marketing spending can produce persistent demand responses, implying that the timing and continuity of advertising matter for valuation (Dekimpe & Hanssens, 1999 ). Recent studies also recognize that the effectiveness of advertising may vary depending on the economic environment and firm characteristics. For instance, Kim et al. (2019) find that advertising has a stronger impact on firm performance during periods of economic crisis, suggesting that advertising can serve as a strategic tool to maintain brand trust and strengthen consumer relationships in times of uncertainty. This is especially relevant to the COVID-19 pandemic context, where advertising decisions directly shaped firms’ ability to retain consumer engagement despite market disruptions. From a managerial perspective, such findings imply that advertising budgets should not be indiscriminately reduced during downturns, as their strategic value may actually increase under crisis conditions. Evidence from business-cycle and recession studies provides mixed but informative guidance: in some downturns, firms that sustain advertising recover faster or gain market share post- crisis (Lamey et al., 2007; Tellis & Tellis, 2009), whereas in other situations constrained demand reduces advertising effectiveness. Semenov and Randrianasolo (2023) further argue that firm age and cultural communication styles play an important role in enhancing firm performance. They view advertising expenditure not simply as a resource, but as an investment in building advertising capabilities. In the Korean context, several empirical studies examine the relationship between advertising expenditures and firm performance or value. Song et al. (2018) analyze the effects of advertising and R&D spending on financial performance for listed Korean firms. Lee et al. (2016) report that while advertising does not have a significant long-term impact in manufacturing firms, it positively affects profitability and firm value in service firms. Additionally, Kwon (2020) examines the state of Korea’s media and advertising industry during the COVID-19 pandemic, reporting a sharp decline in the TV advertising market, along with contractions in mobile and online advertising markets. These domestic findings underscore the importance of industry- and country-specific channels, reinforcing the need to examine both international evidence and Korean market dynamics in a unified framework. Overall, prior studies provide strong empirical evidence that advertising expenditures influence firm value (Joshi and Hanssens, 2010; Chauvin and Hirschey, 1993), and that the strength and nature of this effect vary depending on industry characteristics, external conditions (e.g., economic crises), and firm-specific financial attributes. To identify the net effect of advertising intensity on market valuation, it is therefore important to control for firm financial structure and asset composition—variables that capture leverage, agency environment, growth opportunities, and the relative importance of intangible versus tangible assets. Building upon this body of literature, the present study examines how the relationship between advertising expenditure and firm value changes over time by segmenting the analysis period (2018–2023) into three phases: pre-COVID-19, during COVID-19, and post-COVID-19. By incorporating interaction terms for each time phase, this study aims to identify how external shocks alter the effectiveness of advertising expenditure and to address theoretical gaps in the existing literature. 3. Hypothesis Development and Research Model 3.1. Hypothesis development This study empirically investigates the effect of corporate advertising expenditures on firm value and examines how the external shock of the COVID-19 pandemic moderates this relationship. In general, advertising serves as a key marketing tool that enhances brand awareness and consumer preference (Aaker and Jacobson, 1994; Keller, 1993), thereby contributing to increased sales and improved market value. Accordingly, advertising expenditures are expected to be positively associated with firm value (Joshi and Hanssens, 2010). Based on this theoretical foundation, the first hypothesis (H1) is formulated as follows: Hypothesis 1 (H1): Advertising expenditure is significantly associated with firm value. This hypothesis builds on prior theories and empirical findings suggesting that advertising improves consumer perceptions of products or services and expands market share, ultimately increasing the firm’s market value over the long term (Aaker and Jacobson, 1994; Joshi and Hanssens, 2010). This study uses Tobin’s Q as a proxy for firm value to examine the impact of advertising expenditures. Meanwhile, the COVID-19 pandemic, which spreads globally beginning in 2020, brings about significant changes in consumer behavior, corporate strategies, and overall market structures (Donthu and Gustafsson, 2020; Sheth, 2020). During the pandemic, some industries experience a decline in the effectiveness of advertising or are forced to completely revise their advertising strategies. Conversely, some firms successfully leverage online platforms and digital advertising to create new https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj Kwon (2026) 4 opportunities (PwC, 2021; Accenture, 2021). COVID-19 thus serves as a significant external factor that may influence the relationship between advertising and firm value, and its potential moderating effect warrants empirical investigation (Kim et al., 2019). Accordingly, the second hypothesis (H2) is proposed as follows: Hypothesis 2 (H2): COVID-19 significantly moderates the relationship between advertising expenditure and firm value. In other words, the effect of advertising on firm value may vary across different periods before, during, and after the outbreak of COVID-19. These variations may stem from changes in the business environment, consumer behavior, and advertising media usage during the pandemic. To empirically test this, the study introduces interaction terms between advertising expenditure and time dummy variables (DUM1, DUM2, DUM3), representing the pre-COVID-19 period (2018–2019), the COVID-19 period (2020–2021), and the post-COVID-19 period (2022–2023), respectively. Through this research design, the study aims to explore the association between advertising expenditure and firm value and to quantify the impact of an exogenous shock—namely, the COVID-19 pandemic—on the effectiveness of advertising. The findings are expected to provide meaningful insights into how advertising strategies contribute to firm value even in abnormal circumstances such as a global crisis (see Figure 1). Research model This study aims to empirically analyze the effect of advertising expenditure on firm value (measured by Tobin’s Q), with a particular focus on how this relationship varies across different periods—pre-COVID-19, during COVID-19, and post-COVID- 19. Advertising generally serves as a key mechanism for providing information and signaling product quality (Milgrom and Roberts, 1986; Nelson, 1974) and has long been regarded as a major contributor to enhancing market value (Aaker and Jacobson, 1994; Chauvin and Hirschey, 1993; Joshi and Hanssens, 2010). To examine these effects, four regression models are developed. These models include interaction terms between advertising expenditure and time-specific dummy variables, allowing for a comparative analysis of advertising effectiveness over time. The modeling approach is grounded in the information perspective of Lev and Thiagarajan (1993), which considers advertising as a core explanatory variable of a firm’s intrinsic value. Research Model 1 serves as the baseline model, assessing the overall impact of advertising expenditure (AD) on firm value. It includes a comprehensive set of control variables to isolate the pure effect of advertising (Barth et al., 2001; Chan et al., 2001). Research Model 2 incorporates a dummy variable (DUM1) and its interaction with advertising to compare the effectiveness of advertising expenditure before COVID-19 (2018–2019) and during the pandemic (2020–2021). This model captures the impact of pandemic-induced changes in consumer behavior and corporate strategies (Donthu and Gustafsson, 2020; Sheth, 2020; PwC, 2021; Accenture, 2021). Research Model 3 introduces another dummy variable (DUM2) and interaction term to compare the advertising effect during COVID-19 (2020–2021) and the post-COVID-19 period (2022–2023), in response to potential shifts in advertising strategies and consumer responses in the aftermath of the pandemic (Semenov and Randrianasolo, 2023; Kim et al., 2019). Research Model 4 compares the long-term differences in advertising effectiveness between the pre-COVID-19 (2018– 2019) and post-COVID-19 (2022–2023) periods. This approach is suitable for assessing persistent changes in the market's perception of non-financial information such as advertising (McAlister et al., 2007). All four models include a common set of control variables to account for firm-specific financial characteristics. These variables include leverage (LEV), ownership concentration (TOP), foreign ownership (FOR), market-to-book ratio (MTB), internal cash flow (ICF), return on assets (ROA), sales growth (GRW), the ratio of intangible assets (INTAN), the ratio of tangible assets (PPE), firm age (AGE), as well as industry and year fixed effects (ID, YD) (Lev and Thiagarajan, 1993; Barth et al., 2001). https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj Kwon (2026) 5 The inclusion of INTAN and PPE is particularly important. Prior studies demonstrate that intangible assets, such as intellectual property, brand equity, and patents, enhance firm value by generating future economic benefits and signaling innovation capabilities (Lev, 2001; Cazavan-Jeny & Jeanjean, 2006). By contrast, tangible assets play a crucial role as collateral in external financing and provide stability in firm valuation, especially in capital-intensive industries (Lang, Ofek, & Stulz, 1996; Almeida & Campello, 2007). Thus, controlling for both intangible and tangible asset ratios ensures a more precise estimation of the incremental effect of advertising expenditure on firm value. Empirical Analysis 4.1. Sample selection Table 1 presents the sample selection process for the empirical analysis conducted in this study. The analysis period covers six years, from 2018 to 2023, and includes firms listed on the Korean capital market. All financial and non-financial data are retrieved from the VALUESearch database. The sample is restricted to firms that meet specific criteria to ensure data consistency and reliability. First, only firms with a December fiscal year-end are included to maintain consistency in reporting periods. Second, firms experiencing capital impairment are excluded due to their potential deviation from typical financial behavior. This exclusion is consistent with previous literature that highlights the influence of financial health on empirical results (Lev and Thiagarajan, 1993). Third, firms operating in the banking and insurance industries are excluded. These firms follow different accounting standards and exhibit unique revenue structures that may distort cross-industry comparisons. The exclusion ensures accounting homogeneity across the sample. Fourth, firms lacking sufficient data for empirical analysis are removed to preserve consistency and robustness in the regression estimation. Additionally, to enhance the reliability of the final regression results, firms with outliers or extreme values are excluded. A preliminary regression is performed, and observations with standardized residuals exceeding ±1 or Cook’s Distance greater than 1 are treated as outliers and removed from the final dataset (Hair et al., 2010). After applying these criteria, the final sample consists of 11,424 firm-year observations. This rigorous sample selection process enhances the internal validity of the study and supports the generalizability of the empirical findings. https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj Kwon (2026) 6 Table 1 Sample selection. This descriptive analysis provides preliminary insight into how advertising expenditure (AD) may relate to firm value (TQ). The wide variation in AD and other financial indicators implies that the impact of advertising on firm performance may be heterogeneous across firms. The following regression analysis aims to explore these relationships more rigorously and derive implications for firm valuation (Donthu and Gustafsson, 2020; Sheth, 2020; PwC, 2021; Accenture, 2021). Correlation analysis Table 3 presents the results of the correlation analysis between the independent and dependent variables used in this study. Pearson correlation coefficients appear below the diagonal, while Spearman correlation coefficients appear above the diagonal. Pearson correlation measures the linear relationship between variables (Cohen et al., 2003), whereas Spearman correlation identifies the monotonic relationship between quantitative or ordinal variables (Mukaka, 2012). https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj Kwon (2026) 7 The Pearson correlation results reveal a significant positive correlation between firm value (TQ) and advertising expenditures (AD) (r = 0.10963, p < 0.0001), suggesting that higher advertising spending associates with higher firm value. Leverage (LEV) demonstrates a negative correlation with firm value (r = -0.04043, p < 0.0001), indicating that greater financial risk may reduce firm value. Firm size (TOP) (r = 0.02962, p = 0.0015) and foreign ownership (FOR) (r = 0.06458, p < 0.0001) also maintain significant positive correlations with firm value, suggesting that larger firms and those with substantial foreign investment enjoy stronger market valuation. The market-to-book ratio (MTB) shows a moderate positive correlation with firm value (r = 0.07927, p < 0.0001), reflecting favorable investor sentiment. Internal cash flow (ICF) is negatively correlated with firm value (r = -0.17409, p < 0.0001), while return on assets (ROA) also shows a negative correlation (r = -0.04508, p < 0.0001), which contrasts with general expectations and may reflect firm- level inefficiencies or structural issues. Variables such as sales growth (GRW), interest coverage ratio (INT), and the property, plant, and equipment ratio (PPE) show no significant or only weak correlations with firm value. Firm age (AGE) reveals a modest positive correlation (r = 0.03871, p < 0.0001). The Spearman correlation results reinforce these findings. Advertising expenditures exhibit a significant positive association with firm value (ρ = 0.16188, p < 0.0001). The market-to-book ratio displays an exceptionally strong correlation with firm value (ρ = 0.97738, p < 0.0001), underlining its role in market-based firm evaluation. Internal cash flow (ρ = -0.05789, p < 0.0001) and firm age (ρ = -0.1122, p < 0.0001) show negative associations with firm value. Interestingly, ROA does not exhibit a significant Spearman correlation (ρ = -0.00794, p = 0.3962), suggesting the need for further investigation. Correlation analysis alone does not imply causality. Therefore, further regression analysis is necessary to examine the actual effect of advertising on firm value while accounting for the influence of other control variables (Wooldridge, 2013). Conclusions This study analyzes the impact of advertising expenses on corporate value (Tobin's Q) for Korean listed companies from 2018 to 2023. The analysis is divided into three periods: pre-COVID-19 (2018–2019), during COVID-19 (2020–2021), and post- COVID-19 (2022–2023), to empirically examine the differences in the effects across these periods. To this end, four research https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj Kwon (2026) 12 models are established. Research model 1 analyzes the impact of advertising expenses over the entire period, while Research models 2 to 4 incorporate dummy variables and interaction terms to examine the effect of advertising expenses across the COVID-19 periods. The empirical analysis uses data from 11,424 firm-year observations of non-financial firms listed on the Korean capital market from 2018 to 2023, for which financial data required for the analysis is available. The empirical results are as follows: Advertising Expenses and Corporate Value: Advertising expenses have a statistically significant positive effect on corporate value over the entire study period. This result aligns with previous studies, which suggest that advertising enhances corporate value through brand equity, customer loyalty, and increased sales (Song et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2016; Semenov and Randrianasolo, 2023). Effect of Advertising Expenses During the Pandemic (2020–2021): The positive impact of advertising is stronger during the COVID-19 pandemic, highlighting its role as a strategic communication and signaling tool amid uncertainty. Firms that maintained or strategically increased advertising budgets were better able to sustain consumer engagement, brand presence, and market valuation (Tellis & Tellis, 2009; Lamey et al., 2007). This underscores the managerial implication that cutting advertising during crises may harm long-term firm value, while targeted investment can serve as both a value-creation and risk-management tool (Semenov and Randrianasolo, 2023). Effect of Advertising Expenses Post-Pandemic (2022–2023): In the post-pandemic period, the interaction effect between advertising expenses and corporate value appears negative, indicating that the impact of advertising on corporate value is weaker compared to the pandemic period. This suggests that the effectiveness of advertising may vary depending on external environmental changes, and firms need to adopt flexible advertising strategies that can respond to these changes, rather than relying on fixed strategies. Other Financial Characteristics: Beyond advertising expenses, various financial and firm-specific factors significantly influence corporate value. These include leverage, foreign ownership, market-to-book ratio (MTB), internal cash flow (ICF), return on assets (ROA), intangible assets ratio (INT), tangible assets ratio (PPE), and firm age (AGE). The inclusion of intangible and tangible asset ratios is particularly important because they capture firm-specific capabilities and resource endowments that may interact with advertising effectiveness, shaping its impact on market valuation (Hall, 1993; Corrado et al., 2005). This highlights the necessity of considering a firm’s overall financial structure and asset composition when interpreting the effect of advertising expenditures. Overall, this study provides practical and timely implications for advertising strategy formulation. By empirically demonstrating how external shocks such as the COVID-19 pandemic affect the effectiveness of advertising, the study underscores the need for adaptive, data-driven advertising strategies that can sustain firm value under varying market conditions. Firms should treat advertising as both a value-creating and risk-managing tool, ensuring that investments are strategically targeted and responsive to external changes. Future research should further explore industry-specific differences, qualitative aspects of advertising (e.g., brand image, message creativity), or differences in advertising types (e.g., online advertising) to more precisely analyze the effectiveness of advertising strategies. Additionally, comparative analysis with multinational corporations could help draw generalizable conclusions for future studies. JSON: Name: ad_value_relevance_covid_korea Title: Panel regression analysis of the time-varying value relevance of advertising expenditures on firm market valuation across COVID-19 phases in Korean listed non-financial firms Short Hypothesis: An increase in advertising intensity (advertising expenditure divided by sales) causes an increase in firm market valuation (Tobin's Q), and the marginal positive effect of advertising intensity is larger during the COVID-19 period (2020–2021) than in the pre-pandemic (2018–2019) and post-pandemic (2022–2023) periods. Related Work: Existing empirical approaches estimate the relationship between advertising spending and firm performance using cross-sectional OLS, pooled panel regressions with fixed effects, event-study designs, advertising-stock models, marketing-mix time-series, and occasional instrumental-variable or dynamic panel methods. Prior work establishes positive associations between advertising and sales, brand equity, and sometimes market valuation, but methods diverge in how they handle persistence (advertising stock), temporal heterogeneity, and endogeneity. Common limitations are: (1) reliance on aggregate or single-period regressions that do not model time-varying treatment effects across distinct macro phases; (2) weak treatment of endogeneity and reverse causality (few strong instruments and limited use of dynamic GMM); (3) measurement and reporting heterogeneity of advertising and intangible assets across firms and industries; (4) limited crisis-period analyses that fail to compare pre-, during-, and post-crisis marginal effects within a unified panel framework; and (5) sparse channel- or format-specific advertising data. These gaps reduce causal interpretability and limit insights about how external shocks moderate advertising's value relevance. Abstract: This research examines whether and how corporate advertising intensity affects firm market valuation and how that effect changes across pre-pandemic, pandemic, and post-pandemic phases of COVID-19. Using a firm-year panel of Korean listed non-financial firms (2018–2023), the study operationalizes advertising intensity as advertising expense divided by sales and firm value as Tobin’s Q. The approach estimates panel regression models with firm and year fixed effects, explicit interaction terms between advertising intensity and period dummies (pre, during, post COVID-19), and a comprehensive set of firm-level controls including leverage, ownership, profitability, growth, and asset composition. To address endogeneity concerns, the empirical pipeline includes lagged-ad specifications, industry-level advertising shocks as instruments, and dynamic panel estimators. The main contribution is a time-varying, causally-oriented quantification of advertising’s marginal effect on market valuation under differing macro conditions. Expected outcomes are (1) a positive baseline effect of advertising on Tobin’s Q, (2) an amplified marginal effect during the COVID-19 period, and (3) attenuated marginal returns after the pandemic, providing actionable evidence for adaptive advertising strategy under external shocks. Experiments: Datasets: firm-year panel from VALUESearch covering 2018–2023 for Korean listed non-financial firms; apply filters: December fiscal year-end, exclude banks/insurance, exclude firms with capital impairment, require complete financial fields; report full-sample N=11,424 firm-years and final estimation samples after outlier removal (expected ~10,600–7,100 depending on subsample). Variable construction: AD = advertising expense / sales; TQ = market value of equity / book value of total assets; controls = LEV, TOP, FOR, MTB, ICF, ROA, GRW, INTAN, PPE, AGE; create period dummies pre(2018–2019), during(2020–2021), post(2022–2023). Baselines: (A) pooled OLS with industry and year dummies; (B) firm fixed-effects panel OLS with clustered SE by firm; (C) models with AD*period interaction terms (three comparisons as in models 2–4); (D) dynamic Arellano-Bond (difference GMM) including lagged TQ; (E) IV specification using industry-year advertising shocks (aggregate industry ad growth excluding focal firm) with first-stage F-statistics reported. Evaluation metrics: statistical significance (t-stats and p-values), estimated marginal effects of AD on TQ by period with 95% CIs, adjusted R^2, AIC/BIC for model comparison, RMSE for out-of-sample one-step-ahead predictions (time-series cross-validation by year), first-stage F-stat and Hansen/J-test for IV validity. Experimental setup: estimate each specification on full sample and on three subsamples (pre, during, post); cluster standard errors at firm level; perform placebo tests by assigning placebo period dummies (shifted years) and by using pre-trend checks. Ablation and comparisons: (1) remove INTAN and PPE from controls; (2) replace AD with log(1+AD) and with binary AD>0; (3) drop industry fixed effects; (4) vary outlier thresholds (standardized residuals ±1, ±2, Cook’s D>1); (5) compare OLS FE vs. dynamic GMM vs. IV estimates to assess robustness to endogeneity. Subsample analyses: split by industry advertising intensity quartiles, by firm size terciles, and by foreign ownership quartiles. Report effect sizes (percentage change in TQ for one-standard-deviation increase in AD) and statistical power calculations for key contrasts. Risk Factors and Limitations: Endogeneity: reverse causality (higher Tobin’s Q may enable more advertising) and omitted time-varying confounders can bias OLS estimates; instruments may be weak or invalid (low first-stage F or failing overidentification tests). Measurement error: advertising expenditures may be misreported, aggregated across channels, or delayed, leading to attenuation bias; many zero or near-zero AD observations cause skewness. Sample and selection bias: excluding firms without December year-ends and firms with missing data creates survivorship and reporting-sample bias limiting representativeness. Heterogeneity and generalization: results from Korean listed non-financial firms may not generalize to other countries, private firms, or firms with different media mixes; industry heterogeneity may produce divergent effects that aggregate estimates mask. Temporal confounding: concurrent macro shocks (monetary/fiscal interventions, sector-specific demand shifts) during COVID-19 may confound period comparisons. Statistical limitations: clustering at firm level may underestimate cross-sectional correlation across firms within industries; dynamic GMM may suffer from instrument proliferation and finite-sample bias. Power and small-sample strata: some industry or subgroup analyses may have low sample sizes reducing statistical power. Computation and data limits: channel-level advertising data and creative/content quality measures are unavailable, constraining causal interpretation to expenditure intensity rather than advertising effectiveness or composition.
